judgment.rationale: Both are Content SFIs under the same Competency C-3.3 ('Recognizes and creates symmetry... in familiar two- and three-dimensional shapes') and CG-3. The second SFI (Class-3, rank 2) is informal, perceptual exposure: 'Appreciates symmetry through examples in nature' (LC: appreciate symmetry through examples in nature). The first SFI (Class-4, rank 3) formalises this into 'Lines of Symmetry', whose LCs require recognizing lines of symmetry in familiar 2D shapes and creating symmetrical forms using lines of symmetry. This is substantive extension from informal recognition of symmetry in the environment to identifying and using an explicit geometric construct, so proficiency at Class-3 supports success at Class-4; direction is lower-to-higher rank (second_to_first), which is the only permitted developmental direction. Source excerpts for both endpoints are truncated and both carry merge/audit context (duplicate window extraction), but the retained descriptions and LCs are consistent and sufficient for this judgment.

judgment.rationale: Both Content SFIs are Class-2 bullets (rank 1, no rank gap) under the same Competency C-1.10 ('Compare sequences and cycles of events and describe their duration using familiar units of time including years, months, weeks, days and hours'). 'Months of the year' (LCs: name months in sequence; describe duration of events using months as a unit) and 'Days of the week' (LC: describe the sequence and cycle of the days of the week) are complementary calendar-cycle units of time taught within the same competency and source row: the same skill of naming and sequencing a repeating time cycle applied to two different units. This is substantive same-topic coherence and mutual reinforcement, but the bounded evidence gives no pair-specific indication that proficiency with one unit is required for or developmentally supports the other at the same class rank, so a symmetric relatesTo is the supported judgment rather than a directional buildsTowards. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each), which does not alter this reading of the visible bullet text and LCs.

judgment.rationale: Both are Content bullets under Competency C-5.3 ('Chooses suitable methods - mental computation, estimation or written calculation - for working with numbers, depending on the context') within CG-5. 'Multiple ways of adding' is resolved to Class-3 (rank 2) with LCs covering adding by mental computation, estimation and written calculation; 'Multiple ways of division' is resolved to Class-5 (rank 4) with LCs on solving division problems by more than one method and choosing a suitable method for the context. The earlier bullet establishes the strategy repertoire and method-selection habit on the simpler operation; that flexible-computation proficiency plausibly supports success in applying and selecting among multiple division methods at the higher class rank, so the direction is lower-to-higher (second to first). This is substantive extension to a more complex operation plus explicit context-based method choice, not mere wording repetition; token/page-proximity signals alone were not treated as evidence. Both endpoints carry upstream audit/merge context and truncated source evidence, and the shared Competency and Curricular Goal ancestors lack developmental coordinates, so they serve only as context.

judgment.rationale: Both are Content SFIs under Curricular Goal CG-3 (attributes of 2D/3D shapes, spatial relationships and symmetry). The Class-4 item (rank 3, 'Growing patterns using symmetry', C-3.4 'Identifies, describes, and extends patterns in two-and three dimensional shapes') has LCs for identifying, describing and extending symmetry-based growing patterns; the Class-5 item (rank 4, 'Creating and extending tiling and tessellation patterns') has LCs for creating and extending tiling/tessellation patterns. The later work extends pattern recognition/extension from linear growing patterns with symmetry to plane-filling tessellations that must also be generated, a substantive increase in geometric complexity and productive demand; facility with recognising and extending symmetric growing patterns plausibly supports success with creating and extending tessellations. Direction is lower-to-higher rank (Class-4 to Class-5), matching the permitted second_to_first. Evidence is limited to bounded excerpts (source evidence truncated on both endpoints) and the competencies differ (C-3.4 vs C-3.1), so confidence is moderate.

judgment.rationale: Both are Class-4 Content bullets (coordinate rank 3, identical Class-4 value) under Competency C-3.1 / CG-3 on 2-D and 3-D shape attributes. The first names specific properties of 2-D shapes (diagonals of square, rectangle, triangle; circle centre, radius, diameter) with LCs limited to identifying/describing those features; the second is tiling a region with given 2-D shapes (LC: 'tile a region using given 2-D shapes', tags tessellation/tiling/region). These are complementary strands of 2-D shape work — property/vocabulary knowledge versus spatial covering/tessellation — with substantive conceptual coherence about 2-D shapes, but the bounded evidence shows no dependency: diagonal and circle terminology is not needed to tile, and tiling is not needed to identify diagonals or circle parts. Equal rank offers no directional evidence, and the shared parent, shared page 5, and the '2d/shapes' token overlap alone cannot establish developmental order, so the symmetric relation is the supported judgment.

judgment.rationale: Both Content SFIs sit under Competency C-4.5 ('Develops strategies to estimate perimeter ... and area ... for regular and irregular shapes') within CG-4 on measurement. The second SFI (Class-4, rank 3) is 'Tessellations (tiles and cards)', whose Learning Component is explicitly area-oriented: estimating the area of a shape by tessellating with tiles/cards to cover a surface without gaps or overlaps. The first SFI (Class-5, rank 4) extends this to quantified perimeter and area of rectangles and squares using a grid, plus irregular shapes. Covering a surface with non-overlapping unit tiles is the conceptual basis of unit-square/grid-based area measurement, so Class-4 tessellation proficiency supports success in the Class-5 grid perimeter/area work; direction is lower-to-higher rank (second_to_first), which is the permitted direction. This is substantive extension (informal covering to unit-grid quantification plus perimeter), not mere shared-parent or wording overlap.

judgment.rationale: Both Content SFIs sit under Competency C-5.3 ('Chooses suitable methods - mental computation, estimation or written calculation - for working with numbers, depending on the context'). The second SFI, 'Multiple ways of adding' (Class-3, rank 2), has LCs for adding by mental computation, estimation and written calculation; the first SFI, 'Multiple ways of multiplication' (Class-4, rank 3), has LCs for multiplying by multiple methods and choosing a suitable method for the context. This is substantive extension of the same strategy-flexibility skill from addition to the more complex operation of multiplication at the next class rank, and multiplication methods (partial products, repeated addition) draw on flexible addition strategies, so proficiency with multiple addition methods supports success with multiple multiplication methods. Direction is lower-to-higher rank (Class-3 to Class-4), i.e. second_to_first; not mere wording overlap ('multiple ways of'), since the operation and method-selection demand genuinely increase. Source evidence and some LC metadata are truncated, which limits but does not contradict this reading.

judgment.rationale: Both are Class-3 Content statements (same canonical coordinate Class-3, rank 2) under Curricular Goal CG-2 on whole-number fluency, but sit in different competencies: the first (C-2.1, place value/number representation) covers 'Visualises numbers up to 999, learns to estimate them' with LCs 'Visualise numbers up to 999' and 'Estimate numbers up to 999'; the second (C-2.3, operations) covers 'Addition and subtraction up to 999' with LCs 'Add/Subtract whole numbers up to 999'. They share the same number range and are mutually reinforcing — number visualisation and estimation supports and is exercised by computation within 999 — giving genuine conceptual coherence. However, the evidence is a shared goal, shared range and complementary skills at the same class rank; it does not substantively establish that proficiency in one is developmentally needed for success in the other, so a same-rank directional buildsTowards is not warranted.
